claims.text: A 5–10 µm ceramic nitride coating such as TiN or ZrN can be deposited on boride-based substrates by high-temperature CVD or a plasma-assisted process.
The proposed deposition process will produce a dense, well-adhered protective layer.
The nitride coating will form an aluminum-impermeable barrier.
The nitride film will remain stable during exposure to molten aluminum.
The barrier film will reduce direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The ceramic nitride layer will hinder aluminum infiltration into the boride substrate.
The ceramic nitride layer will minimize reactive diffusion between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Borides undergo rapid degradation through oxidation or dissolution reactions in molten aluminum.
Suppressing infiltration and reactive diffusion will slow molten-aluminum attack of the boride substrate.
The coating will substantially reduce corrosion-related mass loss relative to an uncoated boride substrate under the same conditions.
The coating will substantially reduce surface damage relative to an uncoated boride substrate.
The coating will extend component service life by at least a factor of two.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperatures are approximately 700–750 °C.
The coating will remain effective under steady temperatures and moderate thermal cycling.
Severe mechanical damage can compromise coating integrity and reduce its protective benefit.
Unexpected chemical contamination can compromise coating integrity and reduce its protective benefit.
Long-term durability and the quantitative corrosion improvement in production environments are not yet fully characterized.
A coated-versus-uncoated coupon immersion test at 725 °C can directly compare mass change, aluminum penetration, and microstructural degradation.
Statistically indistinguishable corrosion damage in coated and uncoated coupons would falsify the claimed protective effect.
